title: What already happened: the suffix -di
goal: Talk about what has already happened, negate it with *-madi*, and use *edi* for past sentences that have no verb.
bekal: forming *bordim, bording, bordi, bordik, bordingiz, bordilar*
using *edi*, *bor edi*, and *yoʻq edi* for states in the past

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Samarqandga bordim
dialogs.intro: Monday morning on campus. Nilufar sees that Budi looks tired but cheerful.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: What did you do over the weekend?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I went to Samarkand! By train.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: Great! Did you see the Registan?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Of course I saw it. I was really amazed.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: How many days did you stay?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ikki kun. Shanba kuni ketdim, yakshanba kuni qaytdim.
lines.id: Two days. I left on Saturday and came back on Sunday.
lines.literal: two day. Saturday day-its left-I, Sunday day-its returned-I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yoʻq, arzon edi. Lekin nonushta yoʻq edi.
lines.id: No, it was cheap. But there was no breakfast.
lines.literal: no, cheap was. but breakfast not-exist was.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ha, ikki marta! Lekin sovgʻa sotib olmadim — vaqtim yoʻq edi.
lines.id: Yes, twice! But I didn't buy any souvenirs — I didn't have time.
lines.literal: yes, two time! but gift buy didn't-I — time-my not-exist was.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Hech qisi yoʻq. Keyingi safar birga boramiz.
lines.id: No problem. Next time we'll go together.
lines.literal: at-all part-its not-exist. next trip together go-we.

notes: **The -di form means "did" and "have done" at once.** *Bordim* covers "I went (yesterday)", "I have gone", and "I had gone". At A1, Uzbek doesn't separate them — a rare relief.

**Edi is the past form of a sentence with no verb.** Remember unit 1: *Mehmonxona arzon* (the hotel is cheap). Add *edi* and it moves into the past: *Mehmonxona arzon edi*. Likewise *bor edi* (there was), *yoʻq edi* (there wasn't).
**Hech qisi yoʻq = "no problem".** An everyday phrase that literally means "it has no part at all". Its cousins: *muammo yoʻq*, *zarari yoʻq*.
**Sotib olmoq = to buy**, literally "to take by selling". A compound verb to learn as a whole; *olmoq* alone means "to take" and is often enough for "to buy" in fast conversation.

grammars.title: Stem + -di + person
body: The most basic and most common past form. Note that the person endings are **different** from those in the habitual form — this is the only set you need to learn again.
after: **The negative inserts -ma- right before -di**: *bor-**ma**-dim* = *bormadim* (I didn't go). The whole set: *bormadim, bormading, bormadi, bormadik, bormadingiz, bormadilar*.
**The question adds -mi**: *Bordingizmi?* (Did you go?), *Koʻrmadingizmi?* (Didn't you see it?). A short answer just repeats the verb: *Ha, bordim.* / *Yoʻq, bormadim.*

⚠️ Unlike Turkish, **the spelling stays *-di* no matter what**: *ketdi*, *ichdim*, *topdim* — even though the tongue hardens them to "ketti", "ichtim", "toptim". Write *-di*, and say whatever comes out most easily.

grammars.title: Edi: the past for sentences with no verb
body: Every sentence from units 1 to 5 — the ones made only of nouns and adjectives — moves into the past with one extra word.
after: *Edi* takes the same person endings as the *-di* form: *edim, eding, edi, edik, edingiz, edilar*. For *u* it stays just *edi*.

In fast speech, *edi* often merges with the word before it: *talaba edim* → *talabaydim*, *yaxshi edi* → *yaxshiydi*. You'll hear these merged forms all the time; writing them separately is still correct.
The question: *edimi?* — *Qimmat edimi?* (Was it expensive?). Like every other *-mi*, it goes on the end.

sections.title: Telling a story: words that link events

blocks.text: A good story isn't a string of short sentences. These ten words turn a list into a story.

⚠️ *Chunki* stands **in front of** the reason, just like "because" in English — one of the few places where Uzbek word order follows the European pattern rather than the Turkic one. The word is in fact borrowed from Persian.

sections.title: Samarkand, Bukhara, and the Silk Road cities

blocks.text: Saying city names correctly is the fastest way to make an Uzbek smile. Note that the Latin spelling often differs from the one you usually see in English.

head: Oʻzbekcha
Say it
Known as
rows: Samarkand — the Registan, tomb of Amir Temur
Khiva — a walled city in the desert

blocks.text: The name of Imam Bukhari, compiler of *Sahih al-Bukhari*, is the name of this city: *Buxoro* → *al-Bukhāri*, "the man from Bukhara". So too Imam Tirmidhi (from Termiz), Al-Khwarizmi (from Khiva — his name gave us the word "algorithm"), and Ibn Sina (Avicenna), born near Bukhara. If you know a little Islamic or scientific history, you already know the map of Uzbekistan without realizing it.
Useful sentences: *Men Samarqandga bordim* (I went to Samarkand), *Buxoroda ikki kun turdim* (I stayed in Bukhara for two days), *Xivani juda yoqtirdim* (I really liked Khiva).
